verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “My chest has been feeling really tight.” and when asked how long, replies, “About three hours now.”
Patient reports “a little bit short of breath,” feeling “a bit wheezy,” and a “slight cough.” Doctor later summarizes “non productive cough,” and patient confirms not coughing anything up.

Patient says, “it gets a little bit worse at night, but basically just pretty consistent,” not that it is simply worse at night. The claim omits the ‘pretty consistent’ qualifier and overstates the night-time worsening.
Patient: “I had a cold last week... I had a sore throat, I had a runny nose... You feeling better now... the runny nose isn't as bad anymore.” and “The coughs kind of stuck around.”
Patient states, “Definitely not short of breath at rest…,” and confirms again, “No, no, no, I'm not” when the doctor asks if short of breath at rest.
Patient reports exertional symptoms: “When I'm walking upstairs, I do feel like I have a little bit more short of breath than I would normally be.”
Patient: “Yeah, yeah, I have asthma. I've had it for a while now.”
Patient: “And then I have, like, a hay fever, you know, some allergies.”
Patient: “When I was young I also had eczema…”
Patient: “When I was young I also had eczema and I had a milk protein allergy when I was young too.”

Patient: “Yeah, when I was in high school I had to have a tube put down my throat.” Doctor confirms hospital stay for asthma exacerbation, and later asks age; patient: “I think I was like 17, 16 maybe.”

Patient: “you know the Ventolin, it's called Salbutamol. Yeah, I got that one.” and “they ran out and I forgot to go and grab the next one… about a week ago… So you haven't got any… Ventolin at the moment? … No, I ran out.”

Patient uses “a steroid. Clinol inhaler.” and states both inhalers ran out: “I forgot to bring it with me, so I haven't really in the past week because… they ran out and I forgot to go and grab the next one.” Doctor: “So you haven't got any clinical or any Ventolin at the moment?” Patient: “Not with me right now. No, I ran out.”
When asked about drug allergies, patient says, “No, no, not allergic to anything. Just like. Just the dust and stuff, but nothing. No drugs.”
Patient mentions environmental allergy: “Just like. Just the dust and stuff, but nothing. No drugs.”
Patient: “Yeah, my mom has eczema…”
Patient: “…and my dad has asthma.”
Patient: “Well, to be honest, I was away at uni last week and I forgot to bring it with me…” indicating he is at university.

Doctor characterizes this as an “asthma attack” and plans steroids and inhalers, consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation “post-viral” given “you've had this cold… you've got wheezy with a cough.” Severity appears mild-moderate as he is not short of breath at rest and managed as outpatient.
Patient describes prior severe asthma event: “when I was in high school I had to have a tube put down my throat,” and confirms hospital stay for asthma exacerbation.

Patient ran out and has not used Salbutamol and Clinol for about a week: “I forgot to bring it with me… they ran out and I forgot to go and grab the next one… So you haven't got any… at the moment? … No, I ran out.” It is clinically reasonable to infer this non-adherence contributes to current exacerbation.
Doctor links cold to current symptoms: “Well, it certainly sounds like you've had this cold. You've got wheezy with a cough…,” supporting that recent URTI contributes to current symptoms.

Doctor: “I would quite like to certainly get you some Ventolin clinomodulate.” and later, “I think what we can do is… give you a prescription for some more of the inhalers. We can get that to you within the hour, I would hope.”
Doctor: “give you a dose of steroids. So these are tablets which you can take for five days, two tablets in the morning…”

Doctor: “the other thing I'd like to send you is a spacer… it has some instructions about how to use it, but essentially couple of puffs to prime it inside, breathing in and out for five or ten breaths.”

Doctor: “Once you get better from this asthma attack, you can use the clinalmodulate in the morning with Ventolin as a prn. So Ventolin when you need to… If you should start to use the Ventolin more than every three hours at any time, it's a good idea to seek medical attention…”
Doctor: “might give you some time off work as well. You can self certify for seven days, but I think I would advise you just to rest a little bit until you're feeling a bit better…”

Doctor: “Any deterioration in your symptoms, like worsening shortness of breath or just generally concerning symptoms, pain in your chest, tightness, feeling lightheaded, then seek further medical attention anytime, please.”
